受惠於 OpenAI 與 Anthropic 強勁新訂單，Google TPU 出貨能見度已達 2029 年，優於 Nvidia GPU 與其他 AI ASIC（多數為 4Q27–2Q28）。

(2) 2028–2029 年合計需求數量：OpenAI 約 12M（聯發科設計的 8t），Anthropic 約 14M（Broadcom 設計的 8i），兩者需求均呈逐年成長趨勢。OpenAI 採買斷，Anthropic 則是租賃與買斷都有。

(3) 考量供應鏈限制，2027–2029 年較合理的 TPU 出貨估算分別為 8–9M、14–15M、16–18M。市場普遍預期 AI 資本支出於 2028 年見頂，但此規劃顯示 TPU 在 2029 年仍具出貨成長動能，關鍵在於 AI 服務龍頭 OpenAI 與 Anthropic 的直接訂單。

🚨 THE “OVERHEAD SUPPLY WALL” ABOVE SPY IS PROBABLY NOT A WALL.

The busiest price was 767, leaving a massive block of supposedly trapped investors above the market.

The conventional argument is simple:

Those investors will sell when SPY returns to breakeven, creating resistance and capping any rally.

It sounds logical.

The data does not support it.

We preregistered the test, built point-in-time volume profiles and studied SPY, QQQ, IWM and DIA back to 2016.

If overhead supply actually suppresses price, larger overhead volume should predict less upside.

It predicted the opposite.

Across the four index ETFs, heavier overhead supply was associated with greater 10-session upside, not less.

The result remained positive across 20, 60 and 120-session volume profiles and in both halves of the sample.

Positive outcomes: 67%

But here is the important part.

Comparable SPY pullbacks reached any price the same distance above the market roughly 76% of the time.

The volume shelf was not a special magnet.

It was not a reliable ceiling either.

It was simply another price.

"After an exhaustive search, NVIDIA names its next CEO: Jensen Huang." I joked about it Thursday. What it takes and where investors fit with some Fable help:

• Shareholders elect directors. Directors pick the CEO. Jensen's ~3.6% is big, not a majority.

• Time is the ask from @altcap and @GavinSBaker who want a slow search with his return in play.
• Tuesday cuts both ways. The quarter was Jensen's; the $NVDA call is Kress's. Steady may helps board.
• The probes must go his way: @nvidia's review and Congress on Dec. 1 and 3.
• A special meeting takes 15% held a year. @Vanguard_Group and @BlackRock alone top that. Index funds don't typically start fights. Maybe the slide and potential future slide motivates them.
• No-cause director removal takes two-thirds of all shares. A board-backed 2025 fix got ~99% of votes cast and failed.
• Binding route: nominate a 2027 board Feb. 24 to Mar. 26. Vote likely next summer.
• What no letter fixes: a reported relationship with a direct report.

It’s also illegal.

Brev was acquired by NVIDIA 2.5 yrs ago. Going from startup to a big company was a big change. 
Over drinks, I told Jensen:

“This is the biggest company I’ve ever worked for”

He smiled, looked at me, and replies: 

“Me too”

I survived this long at NVIDIA because Jensen made it feel like working at a startup. He understood that layers of a company, necessary for operationalizing work, also suppress information flow. It happens naturally:
• People want praise, so they highlight the work they’re doing well & hide problems 
• People want ownership, so they suppress ideas that don’t come from their org

But at Jensen’s Nvidia you could email 1000+ people at once to force information to flow outside of an org that might be suppressing it. In fact, you are expected to, sending an email with the “Top 5 Things” you’re working on to everyone at once, to force information to flow outside of a bad manager or org who might be suppressing it. I jokingly call email at NVIDIA a “mosh pit”.

He was always chasing information that was stuck in the corners of the company, always learning from the company he was leading. 

NVIDIA is the world’s largest startup because there’s a founder driving it. Taking NVIDIA from its founder is a mistake.

Paul Tudor Jones: Almost Every Big Crash Has the Same Root Cause, Too Much Leverage Somewhere

If I think of some really, really big accidents, most of them have the same underlying reason, same underlying foundation, which is some too much leverage somewhere. Most of the leverage, most of the time, if I think of the big ones, were derivative inspired, either futures or options.

1987, that crash was 100% portfolio insurance, 100%. Had they had limits, which they didn't, it would have been a 10%, maybe 15% max, but that was 100% derivatives.

If I think about 1998, Long-Term Capital, big derivatives, they had a huge balance sheet with a lot of derivatives they were offsides on.

2000 was a little different. 2000 was the easiest bear market I've ever seen in my whole life. It's got so many similarities to right now in the sense that the bear market of 2001 and 2002 were a consequence of all the IPOs in 99, 2000, and then as they unlocked, you just had this never-ending cascade of selling.
